records.name_note: Admissible sources split on both the accepted name and the lead common name. RHS gives the given name, Chrysanthemum × morifolium, Name Status 'Synonym' (plant 208602) and gives Chrysanthemum × grandiflorum Name Status 'Correct' (plant 123406); the grandiflorum record's Synonyms field reads 'Chrysanthemum × koreanum, Chrysanthemum × morifolium, Chrysanthemum hortorum hort., Chrysanthemum sinense, Dendranthema × koreanum, Dendranthema grandiflorum'. scientific_name_accepted follows RHS's Correct name. NC State Extension's dedicated page is still headed Chrysanthemum x morifolium and lists 'Chrysanthemum morifolium' and 'Dendranthema x grandiflorum' under 'Previously known as'. Both RHS records render the common name 'florists' chrysanthemum' beneath their RHS Plant Profile label, and it is used here in NC State's spelling, Florist's Chrysanthemum, which is one of the nine entries in NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list: Autumn Mum, Chrysanthemum, Florist's Chrysanthemum, Florist's Daisy, Garden Chrysanthemum, Garden Hardy Chrysanthemum, Garden Mum, Hardy Garden Mum, Mum. NC State's own lead is Autumn Mum: it is the first entry of that list, and NC State's Description opens 'Autumn mum is an herbaceous perennial in the daisy family (Asteraceae).'
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Chrysanthemum x morifolium page carries the banner "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its Landscape Problems field renders six stacked values: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; its Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous. Inside the page's "Poisonous to Humans:" block, a human-scoped heading separate from the cat and dog flags in the Problems field, Poison Severity is Low; the Poison Symptoms field reads "Stomach upset, vomiting if ingested. Contact with the foliage can cause mild rashes in some sensitive individuals."; the Poison Toxic Principle is "Alantolactone, a sesquiterpene lactone, guaianolide, pyrethrins and other potential irritants"; Causes Contact Dermatitis is Yes; and the Poison Part field lists three parts: Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice. The same page describes the flowers as edible: its Edibility field reads "The petals and flower buds are used to make a sweet drink or a tea in Asia and a wine in Korea.", its Flower Value To Gardener field lists Edible (with Fragrant and Showy), and its Description speaks of "The edible, aromatic flowers". NC State thus names the petals and flower buds as the parts used for drink, tea and wine and the leaves, roots and sap/juice as the poison parts, and says nothing further to reconcile the two. RHS's two records for this plant (plants 123406 and 208602) carry no toxicity field.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous and its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field gives 5a-9b; NC State treats the plant as a garden perennial that 'can be planted along edges, in the front of borders, or in cut flower gardens' and adds 'They work well in containers planted near a patio or window boxes.' Its only indoor mention is the National Chrysanthemum Society category note 'Sprays: Outdoor or interior pot plants with many small heads borne on each branched stem.', a description of one cultivar group rather than houseplant culture, and no admissible source frames the plant as a houseplant.

Name status: RHS gives the given name Chrysanthemum × morifolium Name Status 'Synonym' and lists it among the synonyms of its accepted name Chrysanthemum × grandiflorum (Name Status 'Correct'). The same Description's shade clause is a tolerance with a warning, not a recommendation ('While favoring sunny locations, it will grow in areas with shade; however, too much shade can cause plants to sprawl instead of growing upright.'), so no shade value was added. RHS's two records carry no Position field.

is_edible is true on a condition: NC State's Edibility field names only the petals and flower buds ('The petals and flower buds are used to make a sweet drink or a tea in Asia and a wine in Korea.'), while the same page's Poison Part field lists Leaves, Roots and Sap/Juice and its Plant Type field co-lists Poisonous. records.name_note: The dedicated pages for this hybrid lead with different common names. NC State Extension's Nepeta x faassenii page renders an alphabetized two-item Common Name(s) list, Blue Catmint then Faasen's Catmint, in the same order as its page title (Blue Catmint, Faasen's Catmint), and its Description opens "Blue catmint is an herbaceous perennial, ground cover native to Europe and in the Lamiaceae (mint) family." RHS's dedicated page renders garden catmint as the common name beneath its Nepeta × faassenii heading and lists "Faassen's catmint, mirrinminttu" under Other common names. MoBot's Plant Finder page carries a single row reading "Common Name: nepeta". Blue Catmint, the first entry of NC State's list, is used here; garden catmint is RHS's name for the plant, and Faassen's catmint (spelled Faasen's Catmint by NC State) is the second entry of NC State's list and the first of RHS's other common names.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, RHS, or MoBot) discusses toxicity of Nepeta x faassenii to cats or dogs at all; the NC State page for this species carries no Poison/toxicity section. Toxicity/cat-attractant information for Nepeta cataria (catnip) or the parent species N. racemosa/N. nepetella was deliberately not borrowed. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null.

is_edible rests on NC State alone: its tag row carries #edible leaves and its Landscape Theme field lists Edible Garden, but no admissible page gives a culinary use or preparation, and RHS and MoBot do not mention eating it.

is_houseplant is false: NC State gives the hybrid the Plant Type values Ground Cover and Herbaceous Perennial and USDA zones 5a-9b, and RHS rates it H7; the container use NC State (Landscape Location: Container, Patio, Rock Wall) and RHS (Patio and container plants) mention is outdoor patio planting, not indoor growing.

soil_drainage left null because the sources split. NC State's Soil Drainage field has the single value Good Drainage (no Moist value), its Resistance To Challenges field lists Deer, Drought, Dry Soil and Urban Conditions, and its Description says "Once established, blue catmint is drought tolerant." MoBot's Culture says "Easily grown in average, dry to medium, well-drained soils in full sun to part shade. Prefers cool, moist soils. Plants are not as drought tolerant as many of the other Nepetas." RHS's Moisture field reads Well–drained. No source states a sharp or sandy requirement, so fast is not supported, and NC State's dry-tolerant reading and MoBot's moist-soil preference disagree on moderate.

soil_ph left null: RHS's structured pH field lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral (all three), an open acceptance that includes alkaline soils, so no ceiling can be set from a closed Neutral band; NC State's page for this species carries no soil pH field at all.

water_regime and related day-interval/dry-down fields left null: MoBot's structured Water field gives only 'Dry to medium', a moisture-tolerance category rather than an actionable watering instruction matching the keep_moist/keep_barely_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between enum; MoBot's Culture prose separately notes the plant 'Prefers cool, moist soils,' which does not resolve cleanly to a single regime. As an in-ground perennial, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, and the day-interval fields are left null per the in-ground-plant rule.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' wording is the site-wide light-category legend used across NC State's plant pages generically, not species-specific prose, so it was not used to set an hour maximum.

Mature size uses NC State's Dimensions block for this hybrid (Height: 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in.; Width: 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in.), which matches NC State's Description ("It rapidly forms a clump 18 to 24 inches tall and spreading as much as 36 inches wide") and MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics ("rising to 18-24” tall and spreading to as much as 36” wide"). Two structured fields disagree and are disclosed rather than merged: MoBot's rows read Height: 1.00 to 2.00 feet and Spread: 1.50 to 3.00 feet (12-24 in tall, 18-36 in wide), and RHS's Max Height and Max Spread both read 0.1-0.5 metres (about 4-20 in).

soil_base is garden_bed for the border and mass-planting use NC State describes ('Use it in a border or mass planted in a cottage or edible garden, or in a garden for the blind.'; Design Feature: Border, Mass Planting). NC State's Landscape Location field also lists Container, Patio and Rock Wall and its Description says 'It is also suitable for growing in a container or crevices in a rock wall.', and RHS's suggested locations include 'Patio and container plants' alongside 'Flower borders and beds', so container culture is disclosed here rather than encoded.
Cultivar pages ('Walker's Low', 'Six Hills Giant', 'Junior Walker') and the Nepeta cataria (Catnip) page were not used to source any field, per task scoping.

No admissible source gives chill-damage onset temperatures, day/night temperature ranges, humidity targets, foot-candle light levels, or a fertilizing schedule/strength for this species; these fields are left null for lack of admissible-source support.

unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, MoBot, RHS, UGA CAES) addresses toxicity to cats or dogs for Verbena x hybrida / Glandularia x hybrida specifically, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than borrowed from Aloysia (lemon verbena) or other Verbenaceae members.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source describes growing this taxon as a houseplant. RHS calls it 'An erect to spreading, semi-evergreen perennial to around 30cm high usually cultivated as an annual for bedding, hanging baskets or containers.', NC State says 'Use these plants in the garden border, in rock gardens, as a ground cover, in hanging baskets or window boxes.', and MoBot calls it 'a short-lived perennial that is grown in St. Louis as an annual'; MoBot's only indoor mention is overwintering advice ('Cuttings may be taken in late summer and overwintered indoors. Containers may be overwintered indoors.'), which is not houseplant culture.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's pH tags for this species are Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), but the Acid band is open-ended per the schema's rule and cannot supply a floor, and RHS's pH field for the same taxon lists Alkaline as acceptable, which conflicts with treating 8.0 as a ceiling.

water_regime is left null: no page for this taxon gives a watering statement that maps to the enum. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale; disclosed, not used for keep_moist); NC State says 'They are fairly drought-tolerant once established.' and warns 'Overwatering can cause root rot.'; RHS says only 'Feed and water well'. direct_sun_hours_max is left null because NC State's only hour figure ('6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day') is the site-wide generic Full Sun light-category legend text, not species-specific prose, per the schema's scope rule.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength are left null: no page for this taxon gives an interval, active months or a dilution strength (RHS says only 'Feed and water well'). Clemson's genus-wide verbena factsheet gives verbena-wide timing and a container cadence — 'A light application of a complete fertilizer such as 16-4-8 in mid- to late spring and again after trimming back will revitalize plants, but additional fertilization is not generally required.' and 'Fertilize container grown plants either with a controlled-release fertilizer, or with a liquid fertilizer once a month.' — but it is not specific to this taxon, 16-4-8 is an NPK formulation rather than a dilution strength, and 'once a month' is a word cadence that rule 9 does not allow converting to a day count.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est are left null because no admissible source frames watering for this bedding annual in terms of a dry-down target or day intervals.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. NC State Extension's dedicated Fuchsia x hybrida page lists its Common Name(s) as "Fuchsia" first, then "Lady's Eardrops," so "Fuchsia" is used as common_name here. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives a single Common Name, "lady's eardrops," but that entry is headed "Fuchsia (group)", a page for hybrid fuchsias as a group rather than one headed with the binomial Fuchsia x hybrida, so it does not override NC State's ordering.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Fuchsia x hybrida page tags the plant #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for horses and #non-toxic for dogs in its tag row. Those three tags are the page's only toxicity content: it carries no Poison block, no severity banner, no Problems field, no toxic principle and no poison-part list. The same page's Edibility field reads "Flowers are edible." and its tag row carries #edible flowers; no admissible source addresses eating any other part of the plant (its Fruit Type field lists Berry, Capsule and Nut without calling the fruit edible), and none gives a handling warning.
unknowns: chill_damage_f left null: the only admissible temperature-related figures found are NC State's qualitative 'cooler summer temperatures'/'cool room temperatures' phrasing and its USDA Hardiness Zone rating (10a-12b), which per the task rules is a survival/zone rating, not a stated damage-onset temperature.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: NC State only describes temperature preference qualitatively ('prefer cooler summer temperatures,' 'cool room temperatures'); no admissible source gives numeric day/night temperature figures for this exact taxon.

cool_rest_note left null: NC State's dedicated page does not give a specific cool-temperature dormancy target (only that plants can be overwintered indoors or propagated by cuttings). Missouri Botanical Garden's page does describe forcing dormancy in a 'cool (40s) basement,' but that page is titled 'Fuchsia (group),' a hybrid-group page rather than the dedicated Fuchsia x hybrida taxon page, so it was not used to support this field.
humidity_pct_min/max left null: NC State states a qualitative need for 'high humidity' but gives no percentage figures.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field ('Deep shade,' 'Partial Shade') carries only the sitewide light-category legend's generic hour ranges (e.g. '2-6 hours'), not species-specific prose stating direct sun hours, per the rule against using the generic legend for this field. No foot-candle figures are given anywhere.

soil_base left null: NC State's Soil Texture field lists Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), and Sand, none of which map cleanly onto the closed soil_base enum list, so it was left null rather than guessed.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field is the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0),' which per the task rules gives no usable ceiling or floor. RHS has no dedicated page for this exact taxon to cross-check a pH field against, so no ceiling/floor could be set.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis all left null: NC State's watering prose supports a keep_moist regime qualitatively ('do not withstand drought conditions,' 'will need frequent watering') but does not frame watering by a dry-down depth or a numeric day interval for either growing or dormant periods.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength all left null: no admissible source (including NC State's dedicated page) addresses fertilizing this taxon at all.

RHS was not used for any field: RHS has no dedicated page for Fuchsia x hybrida specifically — only a genus-wide 'Fuchsia' hub page covering hardy and tender fuchsias generically, which per the task's scope-discipline rule counts as genus-level boilerplate, not species/hybrid-specific evidence. This also means scientific_name_accepted could not be cross-checked against an RHS 'Name Status: Correct' field; it is instead supported here by the dedicated NC State page's own H1 binomial.

Parentage background (not a schema field): NC State's dedicated page states "Fuchsia is a cross between Fuchsia magellaniaca x Fuchsia coccinea x Fuchsia fulgens x Fuchsia arborescens." No parent species' page was used to support any field in this record.

soil_drainage left null (the research record's moisture_retentive was removed at landing): NC State's page for this hybrid carries no Soil Drainage field, and its Description says only that fuchsias prefer 'slightly acidic soils high in organic matter that retain moisture well' and 'do not withstand drought conditions'. That is a moisture-holding soil preference, not the explicit consistently wet or boggy cultivation requirement this catalog reserves moisture_retentive for, and no admissible page for this taxon states a drainage requirement that would support moderate or fast.

water_regime keep_moist rests on the page's only watering statement, 'Plants in containers or baskets will need frequent watering and protection from the wind.', which is scoped to container and basket plants (NC State's Landscape Location field lists Container, Hanging Baskets and Houseplants), read together with 'They do not withstand drought conditions.'; no admissible source gives a watering cadence for plants in the ground.

is_edible is true for the flowers only: NC State's Edibility field reads 'Flowers are edible.' and its tag row carries #edible flowers; no admissible source addresses eating the berries, leaves or stems (see toxicity_detail).

common_name Fuchsia kept: it is the first entry of the alphabetized Common Name(s) list on NC State's dedicated page and the name its Description opens with ('Fuchsia is a cross between ...'); Lady's Eardrops, NC State's second entry and MoBot's group page's single Common Name, is disclosed in name_note. No collision with an already-landed common_name.

Citations repaired at landing: two quotes of the <title> parenthetical '(Fuchsia, Lady's Eardrops)', which the page never renders, were replaced with the rendered two-item Common Name(s) list; the three-tag toxicity quote was split into the single rendered tags; a five-sentence water quote that led with a drought trait was cut to the watering sentence; the humidity quote was restored to its full sentence; and the soil_drainage citation went with the value.

records.name_note: Landed with the hybrid sign as Citrus × aurantiifolia, the name RHS gives Name Status 'Correct' on its record 'Citrus × aurantiifolia (F)' (plant 112190). RHS keeps a second record for the same taxon, 'Citrus × aurantiifolia key lime' (plant 171749), with Name Status 'Synonym', and the Correct record lists that string in its Synonyms field. Sources differ on the sign and the spelling. NC State's H1 reads 'Citrus x aurantiifolia' (ASCII x, double i), but its Species attribute field reads 'aurantifolia' (single i). UF/IFAS's Scientific name line reads 'Citrus aurantifolia Swingle.' (no hybrid sign, single i), though the same publication calls Key lime 'probably a tri-hybrid intergeneric cross' of citron (Citrus medica), pummelo (Citrus grandis) and Citrus micrantha. For the common name, NC State's alphabetized two-entry Common Name(s) list reads Key Lime, Mexican Lime, and UF/IFAS titles its publication 'Key Lime Growing in the Florida Home Landscape' and opens its Common names line with 'Key lime'. Both RHS records instead lead with the bare name 'lime' beneath their RHS Plant Profile label; on RHS, 'key lime' appears only inside the synonym name 'Citrus × aurantiifolia key lime' and as the third entry of the alphabetized Other common names field ('Adam's apple, bartender's lime, key lime, Mexican lime, West Indian lime'). Key Lime is the name NC State's and UF/IFAS's dedicated pages lead with.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Citrus x aurantiifolia page carries the banner "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its Poisonous to Humans block is human-scoped: it rates Poison Severity "Low", gives Poison Symptoms as "Vomiting, diarrhea, depression; potential dermatitis. The fruit is edible, skins and plant material can cause problems.", names the Poison Toxic Principle as "Essential oils and psoralens", and lists Poison Part as two stacked entries, "Fruits" and "Sap/Juice". The same block's Causes Contact Dermatitis field reads "No"; that conflicts with "potential dermatitis" in its own symptom text and with RHS's skin warning below, and is disclosed here, not resolved. NC State's separate Problems field renders four values: "Problem for Cats", "Problem for Dogs", "Problem for Horses" and "Spines/Thorns"; its Appendage field lists "Spines" and "Thorns". RHS's Potentially harmful field reads "Fruit harmful to skin with sunlight/skin allergen (lemon and lime-bearing Citrus only). Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" — a fruit-handling warning covering both sun-activated skin harm and skin allergy, which RHS scopes to lemon- and lime-bearing Citrus, a group that includes this lime; it names no pets. Edibility is conditional, and NC State does not state it consistently. Its Edibility field says "Fruit juice is edible and used in drinks, syrups, jams and jellies, and baking. It is used as a sauce over meat and fish, and also in marinades. Also used in sherbets, sorbets, ice creams, and the famous key lime pie.", its Plant Type field lists Edible, and its Description says "All parts of the leaves and fruit are used for cosmetic, medicinal and edible uses.", while its symptom text says the skins and plant material can cause problems and its Poison Part field lists "Fruits" and "Sap/Juice".
unknowns: outdoor_sun_exposure: RHS's Position field lists "Full sun, Partial shade", but part_shade was left out because the other sources exclude it. NC State's structured Light field lists only "Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)", its Description says to plant it "in full sun, as it does not tolerate shade.", and its tags include "#shade intolerant". UF/IFAS says "Trees should be planted in full sun but in locations sheltered from cold northerly winds." NC State's Resistance To Challenges field lists "Heavy Shade" and "Wet Soil", which contradicts that same page's "#shade intolerant" and "#wet soils intolerant" tags and its prose; it was not used for outdoor_sun_exposure or soil_drainage.

soil_ph_max left null: the sources disagree about the ceiling. NC State's Description says "The plant prefers a pH range of 5 to 8". NC State's own structured Soil pH field on the same page lists "Alkaline (>8.0)" and "Neutral (6.0-8.0)", which is open-ended above 8 and has no Acid band. UF/IFAS says seedling and air-layer-propagated trees "are well suited to the rocky, calcareous soils of the Florida Keys and extreme southern Miami-Dade County" and gives iron advice for trees "In alkaline soils with a high pH". RHS's pH field lists only "Acid or Neutral". soil_ph_min = 5 rests on NC State's prose alone. RHS's "Acid" and UF/IFAS's advice for trees "growing on acid to neutral soils" accept acid soils, but NC State's own structured field omits the "Acid (<6.0)" band.

soil_base left null: the only potting-mix detail on an admissible page for this taxon is RHS's How to Grow > Cultivation paragraph: "Grow as a conservatory or greenhouse plant, in a container of peat-free, loam-based potting compost with added grit, in full light, with shade from hot sun. In growth during spring and summer, water freely, and mist daily. Apply fertilisers formulated for citrus, throughout the year, following the manufacturer’s instructions; water sparingly in winter. See citrus cultivation for further information". The identical paragraph appears on RHS's Citrus × limon (F) and Citrus reticulata (F) records, so it is Citrus-genus boilerplate, not species evidence, and it supplied no field. Two of its instructions conflict with this record and are disclosed here: "water freely" in growth, against water_regime (dry_thoroughly_between, from UF/IFAS's in-ground guidance); and fertilisers "throughout the year", against fertilize_active_months (March through September, from UF/IFAS's Chart 1).

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure found ("6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day") is NC State's site-wide Light-category legend text attached to the "Full sun" tag, not species-specific prose, and no other admissible source gives a species-specific direct-sun-hours figure.

water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, and water_dry_down_target left null: UF/IFAS gives day-based watering numbers ("every other day for the first week," "1 to 2 times a week for the first couple of months") only for the newly-planted/establishment phase of an in-ground tree, not a general growing-season cadence for an established plant, and for mature trees it gives only a qualitative statement ("do not need frequent watering"); per the rule leaving day-interval and dry-down fields null for an in-ground shrub/tree unless a source frames watering that way, none were populated.

fertilize_interval_days left null: UF/IFAS never gives feeding frequency in days. Its prose gives mature trees fertilizer "3 to 4 times per year" and young trees "Repeat this every 3 to 4 months for the first year", and its Table 1 gives a "Times per year" column of "2–4" for years 1-3 and "2–3" for years 4-5. No day interval was derived.
fertilize_strength left null: UF/IFAS gives fertilizer amounts in pounds and NPK-Mg formulations (e.g., "6-6-6-2"), not a dilution/strength fraction, so no full/half/quarter value applies.

attracts_pollinators left null: none of the admissible sources' structured attracts/wildlife fields name bees, butterflies, or other pollinators for this taxon - NC State's Attracts field lists only "Small Mammals," and RHS's page carries no pollinator-attraction tag.

chill_damage_f: UF/IFAS states foliage damage "may occur at 30°F (-1°C) to 32°F (0°C)"; the upper end of that onset range (32°F) was recorded, with wood damage/death separately stated to occur below 29°F.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good and cool_rest_note left null: no dedicated page for this taxon gives a temperature band, humidity percentage, footcandle figure or rest period. The only such figures found were on hgic.clemson.edu's multi-species "Container Citrus Production" and "Cold Tolerance in Citrus" factsheets, which mention Key lime only in passing, so they were not used. humidity_need left null: NC State says only "Heat, sun, humidity and drought tolerant once established.", a tolerance rather than a need. RHS's "mist daily" is part of the Citrus-genus Cultivation boilerplate described in the soil_base entry.

Penn State Extension's "The Argument for Houseplants," University of Maryland Extension's "Growing Dwarf Citrus," and UGA CAES Field Report's "Citrus Fruit for Southern and Coastal Georgia" were checked (all admissible domains) but each mentions Key lime only as a brief aside inside a general, multi-plant/multi-species article (fragrance/pollen note, a thornless-variety note, and no substantive mention respectively), not a dedicated page for this taxon, so nothing from them was used.
No admissible dedicated page for Citrus × aurantiifolia was found on plantfinder.mobot.org/missouribotanicalgarden.org, so Missouri Botanical Garden contributed no data.

Mature size: RHS's Max Height (2.5-4 metres, about 98-157 inches) and Max Spread (1.5-2.5 metres, about 59-98 inches) for the same taxon were not used; NC State's species-specific Dimensions block is the anchor. RHS's spread tops out near 98 inches, well under NC State's "Width: 5 ft. 0 in. - 15 ft. 0 in." (180 inches). UF/IFAS describes Key lime as "a small, bushy tree, rarely taller than 12 feet (4.1 m)."

is_edible: true for the fruit and its juice; conditional, because NC State's symptom text says the skins and plant material can cause problems and its Poison Part field lists Fruits and Sap/Juice (see toxicity_detail).

toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's Landscape Problems field (Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Spines/Thorns) and the matching #problem for cats and #problem for dogs tags on the same page. RHS's Potentially harmful field names no pets and NC State's Poison Severity rating is human-scoped, so neither is used for toxic_to_pets. The RHS Potentially harmful wording is also carried word for word on RHS's Citrus × limon (F) and Citrus reticulata (F) records.

records.name_note: Canna Lily is the name RHS's dedicated Canna × generalis page renders beneath its H1, and it is the second entry of NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list for the taxon: Canna, Canna Lily, Common Garden Canna, Garden Canna. NC State's Description calls the plant Garden Canna and places it in the Cannaceae family ('Garden Canna is a herbaceous perennial in the Cannaceae family ...'), so despite its common name the plant is not a lily. The first entry of NC State's list, Canna, is not unique to this taxon: NC State's page for the name Canna under the separate species Canna indica lists Canna x generalis under 'Other plants called Canna:', and that indica page lists 'Wild Canna Lily' but not 'Canna Lily' among its other common names. NC State records the former name Canna x hybrida and says 'Currently, all Canna hybrids are included under the scientific name of Canna x generalis.' NC State hedges the parentage ('most likely the hybrid of Canna indica and Canna glauca or Canna iridiflora'); RHS gives no parentage and instead lists the synonym Canna × orchiodes.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Canna x generalis page tags the plant #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for horses and #non-toxic for dogs in its tag row. Those three tags are the page's only toxicity content: it carries no Poison block, no severity banner, no Problems field and no poison-part list. RHS's dedicated Canna × generalis page carries no Potentially harmful field. No admissible source gives a handling warning or an edibility statement for this taxon.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual and Bulb, its USDA zones are 8a-11b, and its Landscape Location field lists Container, Patio, Pond and Pool/Hardscape; RHS lists 'Conservatory and greenhouse' and 'Patio and container plants' among its suggested planting locations. Growing under glass or in a patio pot is not houseplant culture, and no admissible source frames the plant as a houseplant.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source states a literal cold-damage-onset temperature for this hybrid (only a rhizome winter-storage temperature range and hardiness-zone ratings were found, neither of which is a damage-onset figure), so left null per rule 9.
day/night temperature fields and humidity_need/humidity_pct: no admissible source gives explicit day/night temperature targets or a humidity requirement for this taxon; left null.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives footcandle values or species-specific sun-hour prose; NC State's parenthetical hour range inside its Light field is the site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, so it was not used per the task's explicit instruction.

soil_base: no admissible source frames a potting-mix or bed category for this taxon in the terms of this enum (it is grown both in containers/patio and in garden beds/ponds per NC State's Landscape Location field); left null rather than guess.

soil_ph_max/soil_ph_min: NC State's bands are Acid (<6.0, open-ended) and Neutral (6.0-8.0, closed top at 8.0), but RHS's pH field for the same taxon lists Acid, Alkaline, and Neutral soils as all acceptable, contradicting a ceiling read off NC State's Neutral band top; per the stated rule both ends are left null and the conflict is disclosed here.

water_regime and related fields: no admissible source frames this taxon's watering as a day-interval or dry-down schedule. RHS's Canna × generalis Cultivation sentence ('Water freely and apply a high potassium feed every 2-3 weeks in the growing season.') recurs verbatim on RHS cultivar pages such as Canna 'Champion', so it is genus-level boilerplate; NC State's prose ('They grow best in moist, well-drained soils, but they can tolerate some standing water or drought once they are established.') is a soil-moisture/tolerance statement, not a watering cadence; left null.

fertilize_interval_days left null (the research record's 28 was removed at landing): it came from Clemson HGIC's multi-species 'Summer- and Fall-Flowering Bulbs' factsheet ('Apply 3 to 4 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet every 4 to 6 weeks throughout the growing season and water thoroughly.'), which is not a page for this taxon and returns HTTP 403 to the landing machine, so the value rested on a page that could not be re-read and on no other source. RHS's 'high potassium feed every 2-3 weeks' sits in its Cultivation paragraph, treated here as genus boilerplate.
fertilize_active_months: Clemson only says 'throughout the growing season' with no named months, so no literal month numbers could be derived; left null per rule 9.

fertilize_strength: the only admissible feeding guidance found (Clemson's 10-10-10 rate, and RHS's genus-level 'high potassium feed') states an NPK formulation/application rate, not a dilution-strength fraction, so left null.

is_edible: no admissible source addresses eating any part of Canna x generalis (edible canna references found in searches concern the different species Canna edulis/achira, which was excluded); left null.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. RHS's dedicated page renders the common name montbretia directly beneath its H1, Crocosmia × crocosmiiflora. NC State's dedicated page gives an alphabetized Common Name(s) list reading, in order, Common Montbretia, Crocosmia, Garden Montbretia, Montbretia, and its Description opens 'Montbretia is a hybrid of Crocosmia aurea and Crocosmia pottsii.' NC State adds that the hybrid was first made by Victor Lemoine in Nancy, France, in 1879, and was originally described in the genus Montbretia, which is now a synonym of Tritonia. RHS's Synonyms field lists Crocosmia 'Donegal' and Montbretia × crocosmiiflora. NC State's 'Crocosmia x crocosmiiflora is often confused with:' module lists Crocosmia 'Lucifer' and Crocosmia paniculata.
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State's or RHS's dedicated pages for this exact taxon) carries a Poison/toxicity section for Crocosmia × crocosmiiflora, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than borrowed from genus-level or general knowledge.

is_houseplant is false: neither admissible dedicated page makes a houseplant or not-houseplant statement, and neither frames the plant as an indoor one. RHS files the taxon under the plant-type categories 'Bulbs' and 'Herbaceous Perennial' with hardiness rating H4; NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Perennial, its USDA zones are 5a-9b, and its prose says 'Use montbretia carefully in herbaceous borders of butterfly, pollinator, children's or cottage gardens.' NC State's Landscape Location field also lists Container, Naturalized Area, Patio, Walkways and Woodland, so container growing is listed; soil_base is recorded as garden_bed for the border use.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's pH field lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) for this taxon, and RHS's pH field for the same page likewise lists Acid, Alkaline and Neutral as acceptable, so per the open-ended-band rule no numeric ceiling or floor can be set.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figures on NC State's dedicated page ('6 or more hours...', '2-6 hours') are the site-wide Light-category legend text attached to every plant, not species-specific prose, so they are inadmissible for this field.

chill_damage_f left null: RHS's dedicated page gives only the bare hardiness rating H4, a survival rating rather than a damage-onset temperature, and NC State's dedicated page gives USDA Plant Hardiness Zones 5a-9b with no cold-injury figure. NC State's genus-level Crocosmia page states 'Crocosmia is semi-hardy, injured below 28 degrees F.', but genus-level content is inadmissible for this hybrid and is not used.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are left null: neither dedicated page carries a structured Water/Watering field or a watering-frequency statement for this in-ground perennial; RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' is a soil-moisture descriptor, not a watering statement, so it was used only for soil_drainage, not water_regime.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength, and is_edible are all left null: neither admissible dedicated page for this taxon addresses any of these.

Invasiveness (no schema field): NC State says montbretia 'has become an escaped weed in both tropical and temperate areas of the world' and states a cultivation consequence: 'Maintenance is considered high due to its weedy nature. Care should be taken when disposing of unwanted plants and corms lest they become established.' RHS's Cultivation section states: 'This plant is listed on Schedule 9 of the Wildlife & Countryside Act (1981) as an invasive non-native species. Although not banned from sale, it is an offence to plant or cause it to grow in the wild in Great Britain.'
Toxicity, cultivar ('Lucifer'), and parent-species (C. aurea, C. pottsii) pages were deliberately not used to source any field, per the taxon-scoping instructions.

common_name Montbretia kept: RHS's dedicated page renders it beneath the H1 and NC State's Description opens with it ('Montbretia is a hybrid of Crocosmia aurea and Crocosmia pottsii.'); it is also the fourth entry of NC State's alphabetized list, whose first entry is Common Montbretia. No collision with an already-landed common_name.
